extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, dramatists, students of dramatic theory, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles for composing tragic drama that effectively excites pity and tragic emotion; covers what to imitate, how to structure action, and how to balance moral and sensuous elements. Useful to playwrights and critics assessing the quality of tragic works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitate nature in actions adapted to awaken pity
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic art ought to imitate nature in those kinds of actions that are specially adapted to awaken pity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tragic poet should select actions that, though they may be accessory in nature, are treated as principal ends in the drama so as to best produce pity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making the victim chiefly responsible by inexcusable fault
rubrics_metrics.description: If the unhappy man had cast himself into ruin by a personal and an inexcusable fault, the interest we take in him is sensibly lessened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not base the catastrophe on the protagonist's gross moral failings (feebleness of mind, pusillanimity) if the aim is to elicit pity; examples: weakened pity for Lear because of his own poor judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not derive catastrophe from malicious will or villainy
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet who understands his real interest will not bring about the catastrophe through a malicious will which proposes misfortune as its end; nor by want of understanding: but rather through the imperious force of circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When misfortune stems from a villain's malevolence the spectator's pity is weakened or replaced by hatred; better to have catastrophe arise from circumstances or fate rather than a primary malicious agent (Iago, Lady Macbeth are cited as injuring the work).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer causes that arise from moral duty and conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Pity is most excited when the cause of the misfortune becomes possible through morality, and when the reciprocal suffering comes from the idea that a fellow-creature has been made to suffer (example: Chimene and Rodrigue in The Cid).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters who act from duty against inclination simultaneously command respect and increase pity; this 'double flame' is aesthetically superior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for the highest serenity: reconcile fate with a beneficent order
rubrics_metrics.description: The very discontent with destiny becomes effaced and is resolved in a presentiment or clear consciousness of a teleological concatenation of things, of a sublime order, of a beneficent will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When tragic suffering can be seen as part of a just or ordered whole, the displeasure vanishes and the tragic emotion reaches a supreme serenity (modern art can achieve this where Greek art did not).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid admixture of conflicting ideas and feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic emotion is weakened by the admixture of conflicting ideas and feelings; the charm attaching to it is thus diminished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not introduce ideas (e.g., indignation, hatred) that will compete with or overwhelm pity; such conflicts dilute the emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance sensuous vividness and moral faculty
rubrics_metrics.description: In the same ratio that the senses are vividly roused in us, the influence of morality will be proportionately diminished; reciprocally, as the sensuous loses, morality gains ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overwhelming sensory detail that makes the spectator confuse sympathy with personal affection or reality; counterpose moral (supersensuous) ideas to restore the moral faculty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use general moral truths opportunely in dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: General truths or moral sentences, scattered opportunely over dramatic dialogue, have great charm for cultivated nations and serve to recall the moral faculty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategically placed moral reflections can lift the audience out of mere sensuous reaction and restore a higher sympathy, but beware of authorial intrusion that breaks illusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vividness (immediacy/present action over narrative)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sufferings that we witness affect us incomparably more than those that we have through a description or a narrative; the immediate vivid and sensuous presence of the object is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer showing actions in the present (dramatic/immediate representation) rather than telling them; avoid narrator self-insertion or actors delivering reflections that break the illusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth (resemblance between spectator and sufferer)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary that we should form of suffering an idea of such a nature that we are obliged to share and take part in it: there must be a certain agreement between this suffering and something that we have already in us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pity presupposes that the audience can recognize themselves in the suffering subject—use universally human motives (objective truth) rather than narrowly cultural or particular motives (subjective truth) unless deliberately targeting a narrow audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness (full communication of external and internal causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: None of the external data that are necessary to give to the soul the desired movement ought to be omitted in the representation; a whole series of events chained together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide the chain of causes and circumstances that make the protagonist's feelings and decisions intelligible—show external situation as well as internal motive so the spectator can judge whether they would have acted likewise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Durability (sustain and renew the impression)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideas we receive of suffering should act on us in a durable manner; impressions should be cleverly suspended at intervals or interrupted and intercepted by contrary impressions, to return again with twofold energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use alternation, variety, gradation and measured pacing to prevent emotional exhaustion and to keep the moral faculty engaged in resistance so the struggle between sensuous suffering and moral reaction persists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure as imitation of a coherent, complete action
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy might be defined as the poetic imitation of a coherent series of particular events (forming a complete action): an imitation which shows us man in a state of suffering, and which has for its end to excite our pity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy must represent cause-and-effect linked incidents that together form the whole action, not isolated tragic episodes; a complete action lets us follow natural gradation of motives and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy is opposed to historic imitation; prefer poetic truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy has a poetic end (to move us) and is therefore free in its imitation; it may subject historic truth to the laws of poetry and to poetic truth (natural truth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not feel bound by strict historical accuracy when adherence would harm the emotional or moral truth of the piece; obedience to poetic (natural) truth is primary for dramatic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit tragic subjects to beings like ourselves (man essential)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only the suffering of a being like ourselves can move our pity. Pure spirits, demons, or men without morals are unfit for tragedy; a purely sensuous being can have terrible suffering, but without moral sense it is a disgusting spectacle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose human (or human-like in moral constitution) characters whose mixture of virtues and flaws allows sympathy; prefer 'mixed characters' between utter perversity and entire perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form must serve the end: use form to awaken sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of tragedy is emotion; its form is the imitation of an action that leads to suffering. A perfect tragedy is that where the form is best used to awaken sympathy; the best tragedy is that where the pity excited results more from the treatment of the poet than the theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ dramatic form deliberately—pacing, selection of incidents, immediacy, characterization—to produce pity; do not rely solely on sensational subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prolong sensuous torments but allow glimpses of satisfaction
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to stimulate the moral faculty, the tragic poet should prolong the torments of sense, but also give a glimpse to the latter of the satisfaction of its wants, so as to render the victory of the moral sense more difficult and glorious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage a rising series of torments with intermittent promises of relief to heighten the eventual moral struggle and the audience's investment in moral resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage the struggle between moral and sensuous faculties precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: The great secret of the tragic art consists precisely in managing this struggle well; the artist advances step by step, only strikes with measured strokes, and penetrates to the depth of our soul because he has only stirred it by degrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use measured strokes, gradual intensification, and alternation of ideas/actions to keep the audience's moral faculty engaged without allowing either complete triumph or despair before the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art's aim includes free pleasure grounded in moral conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: A free pleasure, as that which the fine arts procure for us, rests wholly upon moral conditions, and all the moral faculties of man are exercised in it. This pleasure is an aim which can never be attained but by moral means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While art seeks to give pleasure, that pleasure should engage moral faculties; maintain artistic freedom to recreate (not moralizing directly) so the aesthetic effect can in turn strengthen moral sentiments.
